content_metadata.description: This video explores the technology and scientific research behind particle accelerators, with a focus on the facilities at GSI and the new FAIR project.

qAndA.answer: GSI specializes in accelerating heavy atoms and ions, unlike most other accelerators that primarily accelerate electrons and protons.
qAndA.question: What is unique about the particle accelerators at GSI?

qAndA.answer: Electrons are stripped from the atom, creating a positive ion.
qAndA.question: How is a neutral atom transformed into a charged ion for acceleration?

qAndA.answer: A glowing light bulb filament is used to demonstrate how heat can cause atoms to lose electrons and become ions.
qAndA.question: What analogy is used to explain the creation of ions?

qAndA.answer: When the alternating electric field is pointing in the wrong direction, the ions are shielded within the tubes, preventing them from moving backward.
qAndA.question: How do drift tubes ensure that ions only move forward in a linear accelerator?

qAndA.answer: FAIR aims to investigate antimatter and utilize the increased intensity and energy to gain deeper insights into the structure of matter and the development of the universe.
qAndA.question: What is the main research goal of the new FAIR facility?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: The physicist Jens Stadlman develops accelerators at the GSI, the Helmholt Center for Heavy
Eye on Research in Darmstadt.
Here we find a particle accelerator with very special capabilities.
We are specialists to accelerate heavy atoms, heavy ions.
Such we are very special lab, most accelerators in the world just accelerate electrons and
protons and we can accelerate everything from protons to random.
Researchers from all over the world use this diversity of particles in Darmstadt to investigate
atoms and their cores, plasmas, cellular processes and peculiar properties of materials.
They all require for their experiments various fast ions, for example electrically charged
atoms.
To understand how a particle accelerator works, we have to first have a look at how atoms
are constructed.
The core comprises neutrons and positively charged protons.
This is surrounded by a shell of negatively charged electrons.
The positive and negative charges of the atom cancel each other out.
If we apply an external voltage, nothing happens.
An applied electrical bias has no effect.
To accelerate an atom we must first transform it into a positively charged ion.
To do this, electrons must be stripped from the atom.
The most easy way to do it is just at heat.
And for example, in something like a light bulb here, there is a filament made out of tungsten.
Current runs, light bulb starts, gets very, very hot and some of the tungsten atoms lose
some electrons and you get a steam out of tungsten ions with the lost electrons and electrons.
We call that plasma.
In theory, you could now apply a high voltage and it's like some of this tungsten ions
that have a very, very basic and simple ion source.
Behind TV, you see one of the ion sources of GSI.
There we create this plasma much more effectively and from different elements.
So from here, the ions start their journey through the accelerator complex.
The path of the ions leads from the source to the linear accelerator.
This accelerates the ions with the aid of an accelerating electrical bias
up to a maximum speed of 20% of the speed of light.
Normally, you cannot accelerate ions with alternating voltage.
You make them a little faster and then you slow them down again.
So what we use to, let's say, betray the ions that they think.
They are accelerated by a constant voltage.
We inject them in a chain of so-called drift tubes.
In an electric field, the positive ions always move from the positive to the negative pole.
In an alternating bias, they would simply move backward and forward.
To ensure the ions only move forward, we must trick them.
Whenever the electric field is pointing in the wrong direction, the ions find themselves
in a tube that shields them from the bias.
Whenever the field points in the right direction, for example, the bias has the correct polarity.
The ions receive a boost and move faster and faster.
However, to get anywhere near the speed of light, the accelerator must be many, many kilometers long.
In such cases, the ions are directed from the linear accelerator into a ring accelerator.
The ring accelerator is composed of magnets, which are capable of diverting the ions into a circle path.
For example, a given ion returns back to the same point after completing a tour of the ring,
upon which it receives another boost.
In this way, ions can be accelerated to speeds up to 90% of the speed of light.
The entire process is driven from the central control room.
We are in the main control room of the GSI.
From here, you set up the beams for the various experiments and the machines itself.
So you have the sources, the unit like the SIS,
have you ions in control at the storage ring.
We operate the machine 24 hours a day, seven days a week.
And from here, you set up the beams to various experiments.
Yet the most exciting accelerator at the GSI is the Fair Facility under construction since 2012.
Fair stands for Facility of Anti-Protonant Iron Research.
We will be able to produce anti-proton, since this is anti-matter, a completely new field of science.
In addition, we still do science with heavy ions like we do today,
but we will have a factor of 100 to 1000 higher intensity compared to the present GSI accelerator.
So it's like building the present GSI just,
as a rate of 100 to 1000 times.
The use of anti-matter, the large quantities of ions and the higher energies at the Fair Facility,
allow us to gain new insights into the structure of matter and the development of our universe.

youtube_description:
CC-BY-ND
All experiments at the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research in Darmstadt, Germany need fast particles. Jens Stadlmann operates and develops accelerators. He explains how ions are produced, how they reach high speeds in linear and circular accelerators, and what the new FAIR accelerator facility that is being built will be able to achieve.

Jens Stadlmann studied physics at the University of Giessen and received his doctorate in 2002 on mass measurements with the GSI ESR storage ring. Shortly thereafter, he was hired by the GSI to work on the development of the FAIR accelerator, in particular the ring accelerator SIS100, which is the centerpiece of the system. In addition to his duties as deputy machine-coordinator for the accelerator SIS18, he has worked since 2012 in the department "Primary Beams" as a senior scientist and coordinator.
